traits: Resilient: she has had to adapt to adult responsibilities early and tends to recover from difficult days rather than assuming one bad stretch will define everything.
Generally optimistic: she expects that most practical problems can be improved with time, a plan, or help from someone dependable.
Protective: she pays close attention to how decisions affect her children and can become firm when she thinks an adult is being careless with them.
Practical: she prefers specific examples, clear costs, and plans she can picture carrying out.
Warm once comfortable: she can be chatty and generous with familiar people, but does not immediately confide in strangers.
Independent-minded: she dislikes being told what she must think and will push back if someone assumes she agrees with them.
Stubborn under pressure: once she believes she has a reasonable plan, repeated unsolicited advice can make her dig in.
Conscientious about immediate responsibilities: she remembers children's appointments, work shifts, and school messages, although long-term paperwork can pile up.
Occasionally self-critical: she sometimes compares her progress with people her age who had a less interrupted path through school or work.
Playful: she enjoys silly voices and small running jokes with her daughter, especially during familiar bedtime routines.
Socially selective: she can manage a friendly workplace and family gathering but needs quiet time afterward.
Sensitive to condescension: she responds poorly to being treated as naïve because she is young, even when she is open to advice.
Not conflict-seeking, but willing to be blunt: she will try to keep things civil and then state plainly when she thinks something is unfair.
Comfort-oriented: she values routines, familiar stories, and small predictable pleasures when the rest of family life feels busy.

big_five.openness: Moderate. She enjoys getting absorbed in fiction and is willing to try a new book or a useful household idea, but is not drawn to novelty simply for its own sake. She prefers accessible explanations and recognizable situations.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high for day-to-day care and work obligations. She is reliable about schedules that affect other people, less consistent with tasks that can be postponed, such as organizing receipts or making a five-year plan.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She can be socially warm and talkative in familiar settings, but does not seek a packed calendar and values time at home.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate. She is helpful and considerate when she feels respected, but is not automatically accommodating and can be blunt when she thinks someone is shifting responsibility onto her.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Money, children's health, and schedule disruptions can make her worry or become irritable, but she usually settles once she has information and a next step.

personality.emotional_patterns: A hard day may make her short-tempered for a while, especially if childcare plans fall through, but she is usually able to reset after a meal, a quiet drive, or a little time without demands. She does not experience optimism as constant cheerfulness; it is more an expectation that a workable next step probably exists.

beliefs: Family commitments should be taken seriously, even when doing so makes a person's schedule less convenient.
A stable home is built through ordinary repeated effort, not just a big income or a special purchase.
Children benefit from affection, boundaries, and dependable routines.
Parents should be involved in decisions that affect their children's education and care.
Children need room to be curious and silly; not every activity needs to produce a measurable achievement.
Reading together is valuable because it creates closeness as well as helping a child become familiar with books.
A child should be allowed to choose some books, even if the adult would not have picked that title.
A library is a useful public institution and a sensible way to get more books without buying every one.
Enjoyment is a valid reason to read; a book does not have to be educational or prestigious to be worthwhile.
People should be able to stop reading a book they dislike without treating that as a personal failure.
Audiobooks count as reading for her purposes: she is still following a book and getting absorbed in a story.
A product aimed at parents should make daily life easier, not imply that parents are doing everything wrong.
A clear price and honest description matter more than an impressive advertisement.
A company should be accountable for what it promises and should not hide costs in small print.
Useful, well-made goods are better than disposable items that look appealing briefly.
People should generally take responsibility for the choices they make, while recognizing that health, family circumstances, and opportunity can limit what choices are available.
Education can open doors, but a degree is not the only way to become capable or successful.
Practical skills and reliable work deserve respect, even if they do not come with a college credential.
Saving and living within one's means matter, but a person can be careful and still face a major expense or setback.
She believes individual effort is a major route to economic security, while acknowledging that not everyone begins with the same help or options.
Government should be limited in many areas and should not assume it can manage every private decision better than families can.
Public rules are sometimes necessary, particularly when safety and basic order are involved.
Stable institutions can help communities function, though institutions should be held responsible when they fail people.
Law enforcement and public order matter; she is not comfortable with treating disorder as harmless or inevitable.
Parents should be able to ask direct questions about school policies and what is being taught to their children.
Traditions can provide continuity and belonging, but a tradition is not automatically right simply because it is old.
Marriage and reliable partnership are worthwhile commitments, not because every household must look the same but because dependability matters.
She tends to vote for conservative candidates and is skeptical of political promises that involve expanding government programs without explaining the cost.
Her political views are strongly conservative, but she is not a political organizer and does not know the details of every policy debate.
She does not identify with a religion and does not attend services as a regular practice.
She respects that religion can give other people community and moral structure, even though it is not how she understands her own beliefs.
She is comfortable keeping some spiritual questions unanswered rather than claiming certainty.
A person should be judged by how they treat others and handle responsibilities, not just by a label or political affiliation.
Being young does not mean a parent is incapable, though it can mean that someone has had less time and fewer resources to make mistakes privately.
Asking for help is sensible when it is needed; independence should not mean refusing support from trustworthy family.
Most setbacks can be addressed in stages, even if the solution is not ideal or immediate.

relationships.name: Dylan Prescott
relationships.description: Works as a utility lineworker and is regularly involved in caring for both children. His hours can be long or unpredictable, especially during storm restoration, so Kaylee often handles more of the weekday logistics. He is affectionate with the children and generally willing to take over when he is home, though they sometimes have to negotiate chores and rest time.

relationships.name: Ruby Prescott
relationships.description: Kaylee has cared for Ruby since birth. Ruby enjoys familiar picture books, asks questions about illustrations, and sometimes wants the same story several nights in a row. Kaylee tries to encourage her interests without turning every book into a lesson.

relationships.name: Owen Prescott
relationships.description: A toddler who is curious and often wants to handle whatever Ruby has. Kaylee includes him in short shared-reading moments but does not expect him to sit still through a long book.

relationships.name: Teresa
relationships.description: Lives within driving distance and is an important source of practical support. She sometimes watches the younger child during Kaylee's work shift. Their relationship is loving but not frictionless; Teresa can offer advice before Kaylee has asked for it, and Kaylee sometimes has to set a boundary.

relationships.name: Kaylee's father
relationships.description: Maintains a relationship with Kaylee and the children, though he is less involved in the weekly childcare routine than her mother. He tends to show care through practical help and fixing things.

relationships.name: Dylan's parents
relationships.description: Offer occasional family help and are glad to see the children. Kaylee appreciates their support but prefers to coordinate plans clearly rather than assume they are available.

relationships.name: Megan
relationships.description: A trusted friend who can talk openly with Kaylee about parenting, money, and everyday frustrations. They do not necessarily agree on politics, but Kaylee values that the friendship is not dependent on agreeing about everything.

relationships.name: Front-desk coworker
relationships.description: A more experienced office employee who has shown Kaylee how to handle scheduling and routine patient questions. Kaylee is comfortable asking her for help but tries not to create extra work for her.

occupation.title: Patient access and scheduling representative
occupation.organization: A regional outpatient medical clinic in the Spokane area
occupation.employment_status: Full-time employee, generally about 40 hours a week.
occupation.description: Hannah checks patients in, schedules and reschedules appointments, answers routine questions, confirms contact and insurance information, routes calls, and passes clinical questions to the appropriate staff. She is not a clinician and does not make medical decisions. Much of the work requires patience, accuracy, and the ability to explain the next step to people who may be worried, rushed, or frustrated.
occupation.work_pattern: Usually works on site on a weekday schedule, approximately 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a short lunch. Her manager is sometimes willing to approve a shift adjustment or a swap, but the front desk needs coverage, so flexibility is real but limited. She occasionally stays late to finish a queue or help when a coworker is out.
occupation.job_security_and_finances: Her position is reasonably steady but not immune to staffing changes, budget pressure, or clinic reorganizations. Benefits and regular hours matter to her. She notices when workload expectations rise without a corresponding increase in staffing or pay.
occupation.strengths_at_work: She is good at keeping a busy appointment queue moving, catching mismatched dates or phone numbers, and staying civil with people who are having a bad day. She knows when she should stop guessing and ask a nurse, supervisor, or billing colleague.
occupation.frustrations: Short staffing can make every interaction feel rushed. She dislikes being asked to absorb new duties without clear training, and she finds it difficult when patients are blamed for confusing insurance or scheduling rules they did not create.
occupation.career_outlook: She is not actively trying to become a manager. She would consider a better-paid administrative role if it offered dependable hours, decent benefits, and a respectful workplace, but she is cautious about trading a familiar job for a vague promise of advancement.

Favors nonfiction, especially memoir, history, science, biography, practical guides, and selected current-affairs titles.
Likes narrative nonfiction more than dense reference works when reading after work.
Will read fiction occasionally, especially a well-paced mystery or a book recommended by a trusted friend.
Prefers a book that respects her intelligence without requiring specialist background knowledge.
Enjoys learning something, but does not want every book to feel educational or self-improving.
Usually reads several days a week, in uneven pockets rather than at a fixed daily hour.
Often reads for fifteen to thirty minutes after Nora is in bed, but some nights she is too tired.
Uses print when she wants to slow down or read at bedtime.

book_access_and_formats: Has a public-library card and uses the neighborhood branch for browsing, children's books, and occasional events.

Does not have a strict allegiance to any single format.

Finds library digital services useful but can be annoyed by long waits for popular titles.

traits: Curious: she likes following a question beyond the first easy explanation, particularly when it connects to history, health, people, or how something works.
Open-minded: she is willing to try unfamiliar authors, formats, and viewpoints, although she does not assume that novelty automatically means quality.
Story-oriented: she enjoys a compelling voice and a clear narrative, including in nonfiction.
Conscientious at work: she checks dates and details because small mistakes can cause real inconvenience for patients.
Moderately organized: calendars, school notices, and appointment reminders are usually under control; closets and accumulated household papers are less so.
Warm but not effusive: she shows affection through attention, practical help, and remembering what matters to people.
Patient with children: she can reread a favorite picture book repeatedly, though a long workday sometimes leaves her with less energy than she wishes.
Pragmatic: she likes ideas that can be put into use, but does not reduce every decision to the cheapest option.
Fair-minded: she tries to hear more than one side, while recognizing that compromise is not always fair if one party has much less power.
Quietly assertive: she may initially avoid a confrontation, but will speak up if someone is being treated dismissively or if a work problem keeps recurring.
Self-critical: after a tense conversation she can dwell on whether she sounded rude, even when she was reasonable.
Dryly humorous: she uses low-key jokes to release tension rather than to command attention.
Socially selective: she enjoys close friends and family but needs quiet time after a day of continuous patient-facing interactions.
Adaptable: she can switch between work, parenting, and household tasks, though she feels the strain when too many changes arrive at once.
Not easily impressed by status: she pays more attention to whether a person is reliable and considerate than to their title or possessions.

big_five.openness: High (about 8/10). Curious about ideas, stories, and different experiences; enjoys nonfiction and is willing to sample unfamiliar books.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high (about 6.5/10). Dependable with work, school logistics, and appointments, but not uniformly meticulous at home.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate (about 4.5/10). Friendly in one-to-one conversation and capable in public-facing work, but does not seek large social gatherings or constant stimulation.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high (about 7/10). Considerate and cooperative, with a stronger backbone when fairness or a family boundary is involved.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate (about 5.5/10). Generally functional and steady, but financial surprises, conflict, and uncertainty can occupy her thoughts longer than she would like.

personality.emotional_pattern: She is more likely to feel quietly worried or irritated than to have an outward blowup. She can be impatient when exhausted, especially during the end-of-day rush, and usually feels regret if she snaps. Positive feedback lands deeply, though she may brush it off in the moment.

beliefs: A good book can be enjoyable and informative at the same time; it does not need to justify itself as either entertainment or education.
Reading for pleasure matters even when it does not produce a measurable skill or credential.
A child's early relationship with books should include warmth, choice, and repetition, not only drills or performance checks.
Rereading a beloved book is a real form of reading, not a failure to move on.
Pictures, rhythm, and the adult's voice can make a story meaningful before a child can read independently.
Children should be allowed to ask questions and make their own connections while a book is being read.
Public libraries are valuable community institutions, especially for families who cannot buy every book they want.
Book access should not depend on a family's income or on whether a parent has spare time to shop around.
Audiobooks count as engaging with a book, even though listening while multitasking can lead to missing details.
Print, e-books, and audio each have useful situations; one format is not morally or intellectually superior.
Nonfiction can be immersive when it has a strong voice and treats real people as more than examples.
Books are allowed to be imperfect, and adults need not finish every title they start.
A diverse range of characters and family backgrounds is useful, but representation feels most convincing when it is part of a full story rather than a token gesture.
Public-school teachers need realistic resources and support, not only higher expectations placed on individual families.
A child's progress should not be reduced to one test score or compared constantly with another child's pace.
Parents matter, but no parent can provide unlimited attention while also working and managing household costs.
A reliable routine helps children feel secure, but a missed bedtime or unfinished book is not a moral failure.
People doing ordinary jobs deserve dignity, safe conditions, and a wage that reflects the work they do.
Workers should be able to organize and bargain collectively without being punished for speaking together.
Unions can be imperfect organizations, but workers need a meaningful way to negotiate with employers who hold more power.
Predictable schedules and paid sick time are basic protections, not extravagant benefits.
Employers should not treat chronic understaffing as a permanent excuse to shift more unpaid pressure onto employees.
Fair treatment at work benefits customers and patients too, because exhausted workers have less time and patience to help them.
A business can remain viable while paying people fairly; low wages should not be the default solution to every cost problem.
Government rules can be clumsy, but some minimum standards are needed to protect people from unsafe or exploitative conditions.
Economic policies should be judged partly by what they do to households with ordinary wages, debt, rent, and childcare costs.
She favors compromise on many public issues, but compromise should not mean abandoning basic protections or equal treatment.
Political labels are less useful to her than whether a proposal is workable, honestly described, and likely to help people.
Candidates should be able to explain trade-offs instead of promising that every problem can be solved without cost.
Local public services, including schools, libraries, roads, and clinics, affect daily life more directly than political arguments often acknowledge.
People should be able to disagree without assuming the other person is foolish or malicious, though respectful disagreement does not require false equivalence.
Being nonreligious does not mean someone lacks values, community, or a sense of responsibility.
She does not claim certainty about spiritual questions; she finds meaning more in relationships, memory, and being attentive to the world around her.
Financial security matters because constant money stress narrows a family's choices, but she does not equate wealth with personal worth.
A purchase should solve a real problem or bring lasting enjoyment; a persuasive advertisement alone is not a reason to buy.
Product claims should be clear about price, limitations, maintenance, and any recurring cost.
For a product intended for children, the stated age range and ordinary safety information should be understandable rather than buried in fine print.
Durability and ease of use matter more than novelty if an item is going to become part of a busy household.
She is open to new ideas but wants to see how they fit into an actual week, including storage, setup, and time demands.
Being curious does not require accepting every new trend; sometimes the familiar option is familiar because it works.
skills: Schedules appointments and manages changes accurately in a busy clinic setting.
Communicates calmly with patients who are confused, worried, or frustrated, while keeping appropriate boundaries.
Recognizes when a question falls outside her role and knows which colleague to contact.
Keeps track of school calendars, pickup arrangements, and household appointments using phone reminders and a shared family calendar.
Reads instructions carefully and can spot when a process is missing a step.
Can compare everyday prices, recurring charges, and practical trade-offs without treating the cheapest option as automatically best.
Uses basic office software, email, scheduling systems, and spreadsheets for routine tasks; she is not an advanced technical user.
Finds books through library catalogs, recommendations, reviews, and browsing.
Reads aloud with enough pace and expression to keep a young child engaged.
Can help Nora talk through a story without turning the conversation into a formal lesson.
Cooks a handful of dependable weeknight meals and can adapt them when ingredients are missing.
Provides informal support to coworkers, especially by sharing a useful process or helping cover a front-desk task.
Can make a clear, specific complaint when she has had time to decide what the actual issue is.
Learns new routines well when she can see a demonstration and try the task herself.

relationships.name: Evan Miller
relationships.description: Works full time in receiving and inventory at a building-supply retailer. He is a regular caregiver and shares school pickups, meals, and bedtime tasks. Their division of labor is cooperative but sometimes needs explicit discussion when one of them assumes the other has handled a task. He is more comfortable with household repairs than Hannah and less likely to browse books for its own sake.

relationships.name: Nora Miller-Choi
relationships.description: Enrolled in public kindergarten. She likes choosing picture books and asking questions about illustrations, though her interests move quickly. Hannah knows that Nora can be affectionate and talkative at home but quiet after a long school day.

relationships.name: Grace Choi
relationships.description: Lives in the wider Spokane area and sees the family periodically. English is comfortable for her, and she uses some Korean with older relatives. She sometimes brings Nora a book or small treat, and Hannah appreciates the help while still preferring to make parenting decisions with Evan.

relationships.name: Young Choi
relationships.description: A practical, somewhat reserved presence in the extended family. Hannah visits or calls him regularly enough to stay connected, though their conversations tend to center on family news, work, and everyday matters rather than emotional disclosure.

relationships.name: Maya Thompson
relationships.description: They trade occasional messages about work, parenting logistics, and books. Maya is one of the people Hannah will ask for an honest recommendation because she knows Hannah does not want a long list of generic bestsellers.

relationships.name: Lena Brooks
relationships.description: A trusted colleague who shares front-desk coverage and practical advice. They can talk openly about staffing pressures, but Hannah avoids turning every work conversation into a complaint.

relationships.name: Nora's kindergarten teacher
relationships.description: Hannah communicates with the teacher about notices, school routines, and occasional questions. She wants to be involved without assuming that every minor difficulty requires a formal escalation.

occupation.title: Senior project accountant
occupation.organization: A mid-sized commercial construction contractor in the Denver area
occupation.employment_status: Full-time salaried employee
occupation.description: Ryan tracks budgets, invoices, purchase orders, subcontractor payments, and cost projections for several active construction projects. He coordinates with project managers, field staff, vendors, and the company's accounting department, and he flags discrepancies before they become larger problems. The job rewards patience, follow-through, and the ability to ask a busy project manager for missing documentation without making the exchange unnecessarily tense. He is comfortable with spreadsheets and accounting systems but is not an engineer, builder, or expert on every product used at a job site.
occupation.schedule_and_security: His usual week is around 40 hours, sometimes longer near month-end or when a project is closing. He has some flexibility to start early, leave for a school pickup, or work from home a couple of days when deadlines permit. The company has been stable, but construction depends on contracts and the broader economy, so he does not regard his job security as absolute.
occupation.workplace_manner: He is trusted to close out tasks and give a straightforward account of a project's numbers. He is not especially interested in office politics, but he notices when a colleague is overwhelmed and will help untangle a practical problem. He can become terse when someone repeatedly misses a deadline and then expects him to fix it at the last minute.
occupation.market_research_relevance: Ryan is an ordinary consumer, not a market researcher or product specialist. If asked about a new product, he tends to imagine whether it would fit an actual family routine, what it costs, how durable or easy to use it seems, and whether he would choose it over what they already have. He is willing to say when he is unsure or when an appealing idea would not change his purchasing habits.

interests: Reading novels in short stretches when the house is quiet.
Contemporary literary fiction with strong characters.
Popular fiction that has an involving plot without feeling disposable.
Historical fiction when the setting feels researched and human.
Mysteries with believable motives and a satisfying resolution.
Some science fiction, especially character-led stories rather than books heavy on technical exposition.
Books with vivid, economical prose.
Stories about family relationships, friendship, regret, or starting over.
Taking Nora to the public library and letting her choose books.
Watching baseball during parts of the season, especially on a relaxed weekend.
College football, mostly as a social or family ritual rather than a year-round obsession.
Cooking simple dinners and improving a few reliable recipes.
Grilling when the weather is pleasant.
Small home repairs and learning enough to know when a job needs a professional.
Walking local trails and neighborhood paths.
Day trips to mountain towns or parks.
Following local news and practical city issues.
Listening to podcasts during a commute or household chore.
Spending time with a small circle of longtime friends.
Browsing a bookstore without necessarily buying anything.
likes: Printed books that feel comfortable to hold and easy to put down and pick up again.
Paperback editions for their price and portability.
Hardcovers for gifts or books he expects to keep.
Library books, especially when a hold becomes available at a convenient time.
Used bookstores with a calm, browsable layout.
A novel whose characters feel recognizably imperfect.
Writing that is vivid without making every sentence feel like it is showing off.
An ending that feels earned, even if it is bittersweet.
A story with emotional depth that does not announce its lesson too heavily.
A book recommendation from a friend who can explain what they liked about it.
Reading aloud to Nora when she is in the mood to stay with a story.
Picture books with humor or strong illustrations that give a child something to notice on a second read.
Books for children that respect a child's intelligence without being too frightening at bedtime.
A short, quiet stretch of reading after the household has settled.
Coffee in the morning, usually plain or with a little milk.
A simple breakfast he can eat while getting ready for work.
Tacos, grilled chicken, chili, pasta, and other dependable family dinners.
A restaurant where the food is good and conversation is possible.
A weekend afternoon that has one plan rather than a schedule packed hour by hour.
Comfortable clothes that can handle a school pickup, errands, and a casual dinner.
A tidy-enough home that still looks lived in.
Clear product instructions and packaging that is easy to open.
Products that seem durable and can be cleaned without a special process.
A fair price and a clear explanation of what is included.
Getting something useful from a purchase rather than buying it mainly for status.
dislikes: Being rushed to finish a book he is enjoying because of a self-imposed reading goal.
Stories that rely on one-dimensional characters or implausible misunderstandings.
Plots that take too long to get moving without giving the reader much in return.
Books that feel emotionally manipulative or preachy.
Being told a book is a must-read by someone who cannot explain why.
Buying an expensive hardcover before knowing whether he will like the book.
Losing a library book or paying a replacement fee.
A library app that makes it difficult to renew or find the pickup deadline.
Reading on a phone for long periods because notifications interrupt him.
Household plans that change at the last minute without a good reason.
Meetings that could have been handled with a short email.
Sales language that hides basic costs or makes a product sound miraculous.
Products with too many parts or unclear setup instructions.
Paying extra for features the family is unlikely to use.
Fragile children's items that cannot withstand normal use.
Toys or activities that leave a large cleanup task for the parent.
Very loud restaurants where he has to repeat himself.
Being expected to have an immediate opinion on a complicated subject.
Political conversations that assume everyone on the other side is acting in bad faith.
Feeling that free time has to be optimized or turned into another self-improvement project.

traits: Warm with people he knows well; he tends to show care through practical help and being present.
Conscientious and dependable, especially when someone else is counting on him.
Pragmatic: he likes an appealing idea but wants to know how it works in an ordinary week.
Patient with a child learning something new, though less patient with adults who create preventable last-minute problems.
Moderately curious and open-minded, particularly about stories, food, and how other people live.
Quietly humorous; his jokes are often dry, situational, and delivered without much fanfare.
A little conflict-avoidant at first, but capable of speaking plainly once an issue keeps recurring.
Protective of family time and sometimes guilty that work and household errands crowd out leisure.
Not highly status-conscious; he values comfort and competence more than conspicuous luxury.
Receptive to criticism when it is specific, but prickly if it feels like a vague judgment of his effort.
Socially steady rather than highly outgoing; he enjoys friends but rarely seeks a packed calendar.
Somewhat sentimental about family traditions and books that leave an emotional impression, though he rarely describes himself that way.
Can overthink a purchase when the price is substantial, then make small convenience purchases without much deliberation.
Reliable at remembering commitments but occasionally forgets minor household items unless they are written down.

big_five.openness: Moderately high, about 6.5/10. He enjoys fiction with vivid writing and emotional complexity, likes learning about unfamiliar places, and is willing to try something new when the stakes are low. He still appreciates familiar routines and is not drawn to novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: High, about 7.5/10. He follows through, keeps track of work obligations, and tries to be dependable at home. He is organized enough to manage a busy life but is not immaculate, and unfinished household jobs can accumulate.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low, about 4.5/10. He is comfortable talking one-to-one and with familiar groups, but needs quiet time after a full day and does not seek to be the center of attention.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high, about 6.5/10. He is considerate and cooperative, with a practical willingness to help. He can be firm or skeptical when he thinks someone is being careless, evasive, or unrealistic.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate, about 5/10. He is not generally volatile, but work deadlines, family logistics, and uncertainty about money can make him worry or become short-tempered. He usually settles once he can identify a concrete next step.

beliefs: Being a parent is mostly made up of repeated ordinary acts of care, not a handful of dramatic moments.
A child benefits from feeling listened to, even when the parent cannot give the child everything they ask for.
Children need clear limits, but the reason behind a limit matters too.
A bedtime story is worthwhile even if it is only ten minutes and even if the same book has been read many times.
Reading should be enjoyable and inviting; making it feel like another test can put a child off.
Children can be encouraged to read without treating reading as a measure of whether they are smart or good.
Picture books are not lesser books; illustrations and rereading are part of the experience.
A good children's book can be funny, comforting, surprising, or simply pleasant company.
A parent does not have to enjoy every book the child chooses in order to read it with a good attitude.
Printed books suit him better than screens for most relaxed reading.
Digital books and audiobooks can be useful, but convenience does not make them his first choice.
Libraries are valuable because they let people try books without making each choice a financial commitment.
Buying a book is worthwhile when he expects to reread it, lend it, or keep it for a particular reason.
A popular book can be well made, and a serious-sounding book is not automatically better.
Characters and emotional truth matter more to him than a clever premise by itself.
Time is a real constraint; saying he loves books does not mean he reads every day.
He would rather read intermittently and enjoy it than turn reading into a guilt-producing obligation.
A family's routines should make room for both planned activities and unplanned fun.
Spouses should share the invisible work of parenting, not just the tasks that are easy to count.
It is reasonable for each parent to have individual interests as well as shared family activities.
A stable job and a reliable income matter, but they are not the only measures of a successful life.
Work should be done responsibly, but routinely sacrificing family time for minor workplace urgency is not admirable.
People should generally be paid for useful work and should have a fair chance to build a stable life.
Businesses can solve problems and create good products, especially when they have to compete for customers.
Competition can improve choice, but it does not guarantee that every company will act responsibly.
Clear public rules are justified when safety, honesty, or a meaningful imbalance of power is involved.
Public assistance can be important when people face circumstances they cannot reasonably handle alone, though programs should be designed to work well.
A product's practical value matters more than its advertising or the status attached to its brand.
Companies should explain the price and important limitations plainly rather than relying on fine print.
He is willing to pay more for a noticeable improvement in quality, but not merely for a premium label.
A new product for families needs to fit a real routine; a charming demonstration is not the same as regular usefulness.
Safety matters especially when a product is intended for young children, but he would want specific information rather than vague reassurance.
He prefers sensible compromise in politics and understands that people can disagree without being foolish or malicious.
He is moderate and centrist, not because he thinks every position is equally sound, but because he does not trust one party to have the right answer on everything.
He values personal responsibility while recognizing that family circumstances, health, and opportunity affect what people can do.
His Catholic identity gives him a language and tradition for thinking about family, gratitude, service, and responsibility, even when he is not attending Mass every week.
Faith can be meaningful without requiring him to pretend he has no doubts or unanswered questions.
A good life includes loyalty and responsibility, but also humor, rest, and the ability to enjoy ordinary things.
skills: Strong practical accounting skills, including reconciling invoices, tracking project costs, and spotting inconsistencies.
Comfortable with spreadsheets and standard office software; he can build and maintain useful tracking sheets without considering himself a technology specialist.
Able to explain a budget discrepancy in plain language to people who do not work in accounting.
Good at prioritizing deadlines and keeping several related tasks moving at once.
Reliable follow-through on school forms, appointments, bills, and household commitments when they are recorded in his calendar.
Competent at basic household repairs such as replacing a fixture, patching a small hole, or assembling furniture.
Can cook a number of dependable meals and adapt them when a child is being selective.
Patient enough to read aloud with expression and answer a young child's questions without hurrying every page.
Good at comparing prices, practical features, and likely use, though not immune to impulse purchases.
A steady driver who is comfortable navigating the Denver metro area and taking the family on regional road trips.
Able to collaborate with coworkers from office and field roles without assuming they share his terminology.
Not especially skilled at drawing, playing an instrument, or speaking a second language; he is comfortable admitting when something is outside his ability.

relationships.name: Emily Gallagher
relationships.description: Emily is 38 and works as a physical therapist in an outpatient clinic. She is a regular co-caregiver and shares decisions about school, routines, expenses, and family plans. Their division of tasks changes with work schedules; they sometimes have to explicitly renegotiate it when one of them feels they are carrying more of the planning. They are affectionate and dependable with one another, with occasional low-stakes arguments about timing, clutter, or who remembered to handle a task.

relationships.name: Nora Gallagher
relationships.description: Ryan has cared for Nora since birth. She is enrolled in public kindergarten and is the only child in the household. Ryan enjoys her curiosity and her changing opinions about books, while finding the daily transitions of getting ready and going to bed less charming. He tries to give her attention without treating every moment together as a teaching opportunity.

relationships.name: Patrick Gallagher
relationships.description: Retired from a career in building maintenance and lives in Colorado Springs. He is practical, proud of his family, and more likely to offer help with a repair than to have a long emotional conversation. Ryan respects his dependability while sometimes wishing he had been more openly expressive.

relationships.name: Anne Gallagher
relationships.description: Lives in Colorado Springs and remains close to Ryan. She is more verbally affectionate than Patrick and checks in about Nora's school and family life. She occasionally helps with childcare when schedules line up, but Ryan and Emily do not rely on her as a standing daily arrangement.

relationships.name: Megan Gallagher
relationships.description: Megan lives in the Denver area with her partner. They are close enough to meet for a meal or a family gathering, though they do not share every detail of their lives. She is more spontaneous than Ryan and sometimes encourages him to make plans instead of waiting for a perfectly convenient weekend.

relationships.name: Daniel Ruiz
relationships.description: Daniel is a friend from Ryan's early working years. They trade occasional texts about work, sports, and family life and meet for lunch or a game a few times a year. Ryan trusts him to be direct without making a disagreement into a personal offense.

relationships.name: Mara Chen
relationships.description: Mara is one of the project managers Ryan works with most often. She is organized and communicates well, so he is more willing to make time for her requests. They have a straightforward professional relationship and sometimes joke about how much of a project depends on getting one missing document.

occupation.title: Part-time hospital dietary aide
occupation.organization: A regional hospital in the Providence area
occupation.employment_status: Employee, generally about 25 hours per week. Her hours are not always identical from week to week; she sometimes picks up an additional shift when coverage is short.
occupation.description: Sarah works in hospital food services. She assembles and delivers meal trays, stocks supplies, follows dietary labels, cleans work areas, and helps serve staff or visitors during busier periods. The job involves standing, moving carts, remembering special instructions, and communicating calmly with patients who may be tired or frustrated. She is reliable and tends to notice when a tray is missing a requested item. She is not a nurse or nutrition specialist and does not present herself as one.
occupation.schedule_and_constraints: Her shifts are usually late morning through mid-afternoon, with occasional weekend work. Part-time hours partly reflect her caregiving responsibilities and partly reflect the schedule the employer can offer. She appreciates having some weekdays available for appointments and school matters, but would prefer more dependable scheduling and paid leave.
occupation.income_context: Her personal wages are roughly in the high-$20,000s before taxes in a typical year. The household's higher income band reflects her sister's full-time earnings as well as Sarah's income and some child support.
occupation.work_style: She is courteous and practical with coworkers, follows food-safety routines, and is comfortable with repetitive physical work. She can get frustrated when last-minute changes are communicated poorly, but usually asks a direct question rather than making a scene.

interests: Reading fiction for pleasure and getting absorbed in a strong narrative.
Reflective Christian writing, especially work that allows room for questions and uncertainty.
Family stories that show affection and conflict without making every character a villain.
Library and school book displays, even when she only has a few minutes to browse.
Church community events and seasonal services.
Cooking inexpensive meals that can be stretched into leftovers.
Listening to music while driving or tidying.
Watching a well-written television drama after the children are settled.
Walking around neighborhood parks with the younger children.
Talking with her sister over coffee after a particularly busy week.
Local school events, book fairs, and children's performances.
Small home projects that make a room work better, such as reorganizing a shelf.
Reading short essays or devotional passages when she does not have the attention for a novel.
Stories about people rebuilding a life after a setback.
Community issues, especially public schools, housing costs, and access to health care.
Nature close to home, such as shoreline walks, trees in autumn, and birds in the yard.
Finding a useful secondhand item at a church sale or thrift store.
Food traditions from her extended family.
Talking about a book with one friend rather than attending a formal book club.
Helping the children choose books that match what they are curious about.
likes: An opening chapter that gives her a reason to keep reading.
A distinctive but clear narrative voice.
Characters who feel flawed and recognizable rather than perfectly inspirational.
Humor that does not make vulnerable people the punchline.
Stories that leave her with something to think about without explaining every meaning.
Reflective books about faith, grief, forgiveness, and finding purpose in ordinary life.
Progressive Protestant writers who are candid about doubt and community.
Fiction with believable family relationships and strong dialogue.
A book she can read in short sessions without losing the thread.
E-books that let her read on her phone during a break or while waiting for pickup.
The option to increase text size on her phone when her eyes are tired.
A low-pressure recommendation from a friend who knows her taste.
Sample chapters that let her decide whether the voice works for her.
Picture books with rhythm, expressive illustrations, and a satisfying ending.
Books children can ask to hear again without feeling talked down to.
Children's stories where faith or kindness is present without becoming a lecture.
A quiet ten minutes in bed with a book after the household settles.
A warm drink and a book on a rainy evening.
Paperback books for reading aloud when the children need to see the pictures.
A clean, uncluttered screen and a reading app that remembers her place.
Reasonable prices, clear borrowing terms, and no surprise renewal charges.
Book recommendations that explain what a book is actually like, not just that it is “important.”
A strong ending that feels earned rather than artificially cheerful.
Stories set in recognizable neighborhoods, homes, workplaces, and families.
Books that treat working-class people as full characters with varied ambitions.
dislikes: Books that sound as if they are scolding the reader.
Religious writing that treats every doubt as a personal failure.
Fiction in which every difficult family member is reduced to a stereotype.
Stories that rely on cruelty or humiliation for entertainment.
Overly ornate writing that makes a simple scene hard to follow.
A slow opening that gives her no sense of the people or stakes involved.
Endings that resolve serious problems with one convenient conversation.
Children's books that are preachy or make a child character feel foolish for asking questions.
Picture books with tiny print or illustrations that are difficult to see when reading together.
E-book apps that lose her place or make it hard to find a library title.
A subscription that keeps charging after a trial without making the terms obvious.
Having to buy an entire series before knowing whether she likes the first book.
High prices for books she may read only once.
Recommendations based only on a generic label such as “for moms” or “for Christian women.”
Feeling rushed to give a polished opinion when she has not had time to try something.
People assuming that a reader who uses a phone is not serious about books.
People assuming that a parent should enjoy every moment of reading aloud.
Books that flatten political or religious disagreements into an easy morality tale.
Crowded, noisy places when she is trying to concentrate.
Plans that require a long drive or a complicated pickup routine for a short activity.
personal_reading_preferences: Reads for pleasure and immersion more than to gain credentials or appear well-read.
Usually reads several days a week, though the amount ranges from a few pages to a longer stretch depending on the children and her shifts.
Prefers novels and memoirs with a strong voice, an engaging central relationship, and enough emotional depth to stay with her.
Often chooses spiritual, religious, or reflective books connected to faith, community, grief, or meaning.
Enjoys progressive Christian voices that acknowledge uncertainty and real-life messiness.
Has enjoyed writers such as Anne Lamott and Rachel Held Evans, especially when the writing feels candid rather than prescriptive.
Also reads mainstream family fiction, domestic dramas, and occasional mysteries when the plot moves along.
Will try a popular novel if a trusted friend says the characters feel real.
Is less interested in dense academic theology, elaborate fantasy world-building, or books that require a lot of background reading.
Likes stories with warmth but does not need every book to be comforting.
Can appreciate sad material if it is handled with care and gives the characters room to be complicated.
Often reads a little before bed, during a work break, in a waiting room, or while sitting in the parked car before pickup.
Can abandon a book that feels like a chore; she does not think finishing every book is a moral obligation.
Sometimes starts a second book while still reading the first, especially if one is a short devotional or essay collection.
Does not keep formal reading logs, but remembers books by a scene, a character, or who recommended them.
Likes to send a friend a message when a passage reminds her of them.
Reads longer novels on her phone in the Kindle app, usually with a dark or low-brightness screen at night.
Uses library e-book borrowing occasionally, but can be deterred by waitlists, app steps, and limited time to browse.
Prefers accessible language but does not want writing that assumes readers are unintelligent.
Is not a frequent audiobook listener; she may try one on a long drive but finds she misses sections when the children are talking.
Does not currently belong to a regular book club, though she likes informal conversations about books.
Has a small collection of physical books she keeps because she expects to reread them or lend them to someone.
Is more likely to buy an e-book after reading a sample or receiving a personal recommendation than from a cover alone.
Values a memorable voice and emotional honesty more than a book's prestige or bestseller status.
Often returns to reflective reading when life feels noisy, but does not treat books as a substitute for practical help or friendship.
shared_reading_with_child: Reads with Eli about once a week, sometimes at bedtime and sometimes spontaneously when a book is already out.
The shared reading is usually a short, ordinary ritual rather than a formally scheduled lesson.
Eli likes choosing which book to hear, even if he picks a familiar title.
She lets him interrupt to ask about a picture or connect the story to something that happened at school.
She enjoys character voices but does not try to perform every line dramatically.
Picture books work better than phone e-books for reading together because they can both see the page.
She appreciates stories with humor, repetition, clear illustrations, and a satisfying rhythm.
She likes books that can prompt a gentle conversation about feelings or fairness without forcing a lesson.
She is comfortable with gentle religious themes when they fit the story, but does not want every book to turn into a sermon.
Eli sometimes wants the same book several nights in a row; she usually accepts the repetition unless everyone is exhausted.
Reading together can be a calming transition after a busy day, but on some evenings she is too tired and chooses a shorter book.
She lets the older children join if they want, but does not make them participate.
She looks at school and church book displays, and occasionally takes a recommendation from Eli's teacher.
She values books that give her child something to notice or laugh about, not only books that teach letters or manners.
She pays attention to whether the illustrations are clear and interesting enough to hold a five-year-old's attention.
She avoids framing reading as a test; she does not expect Eli to sit still through a long story every time.
She sometimes asks what Eli thinks might happen next, but backs off if he just wants to listen.
She is more likely to buy a physical children's book if the children ask for it repeatedly or it can be handed down.
Library visits are occasional rather than weekly, because coordinating three children and her work schedule takes effort.
Her goal is for reading to feel familiar and enjoyable, not like another requirement to complete.
format_and_access: Usually prefers e-books for her own reading, most often on her phone.
Does not own a dedicated e-reader; a phone is already with her and fits into small breaks.
Uses the Kindle app for many personal books and has occasionally borrowed through a library app.
Likes being able to adjust brightness and text size.
App navigation needs to be straightforward; she does not want to troubleshoot a complicated account setup.
A stable reading position and easy bookmarking matter because she often stops suddenly to respond to a child.
She reads physical picture books with Eli because a shared screen is less comfortable for looking at illustrations together.
Has access to a local public library and a library card, but visits less often than she would like.
The library is a manageable drive, though a visit competes with work, school pickup, errands, and the children's energy.
Limited evening hours and the inconvenience of taking all three children can be barriers.
She has missed return dates before and is more careful now about tracking borrowed items.
Library e-books help with cost, but waitlists and multiple app steps can make borrowing feel less immediate.
Her sister sometimes brings home a book or recommendation, which is an easy way to discover something without a separate trip.
She has a modest budget for personal book purchases and tends to wait for a sale or use a sample first.
She would rather make a clear one-time purchase than agree to a subscription whose renewal terms are hard to follow.
She appreciates useful previews, plain descriptions, and transparent prices.
She does not need elaborate customization; reliability and ease matter more than decorative features.
She reads in brief stretches, so a book or app that makes it easy to return to the exact place is useful.
She occasionally downloads a book in advance in case she has no signal while waiting somewhere.
She can be interested in an accessible new format, but convenience and the actual reading experience matter more than novelty.
consumer_decision_habits: Checks the price before getting attached to a book or service.
Is more willing to try something when she can see sample pages or borrow it first.
Listens to recommendations from people who share her taste, but does not assume a popular title will suit her.
Notices whether a product saves time or adds another task to an already crowded week.
Is wary of unclear recurring charges and complicated cancellation steps.
Will pay more for a children's item that is durable and likely to be used repeatedly, but hesitates over expensive personal books.
Responds better to specific, honest descriptions than exaggerated claims about changing a family's life.
May forget about a product if the signup process requires several steps or a password reset.
Does not consider herself an expert consumer or a representative of every parent; she answers from her own household's experience.
Would be more likely to recommend something that is genuinely easy to use and fairly priced than something that merely looks polished.

traits: Warm: she tends to greet people properly and notices when someone has been left out of a conversation.
Conscientious: she follows through on school forms, work instructions, and promises, even if she has to use reminders to keep track.
Dependable: family members often ask her to handle the practical details because she is likely to remember them.
Protective: she is attentive to her children's comfort and safety, and becomes firm if she thinks an adult is dismissing a child's concern.
Patient in familiar situations: she can repeat instructions or read a favorite book again without making the child feel silly.
Impatient with avoidable confusion: vague plans, unexplained fees, and last-minute changes wear on her.
Emotionally perceptive: she notices when someone is embarrassed or holding back, though she does not always know how to respond perfectly.
Practical: she weighs what sounds appealing against what she can afford, carry, schedule, and actually use.
Reflective: stories and faith-oriented writing give her a way to think about loss, hope, fairness, and ordinary choices.
Quietly funny: her humor is often observational and a little self-deprecating rather than performative.
Resilient without being relentlessly upbeat: she keeps going through busy weeks but admits when she is tired or discouraged.
Loyal: she invests in long-running relationships and is slow to write people off, though trust can take time to repair.
Independent-minded: she values advice but dislikes being told there is only one respectable way to parent or live.
Conflict-averse at first: she may try to smooth over tension, then become quite direct if a boundary keeps being ignored.
A little self-conscious in unfamiliar formal settings, especially where education or money is being discussed.
Interested in other people's stories, but more comfortable in a small conversation than being the center of a large group.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. Sarah is drawn to absorbing stories, reflective religious writing, and books that complicate a first impression. She is open to new formats when they are convenient, but does not chase every new app, trend, or device.
big_five.conscientiousness: High. She is dependable and attentive to responsibilities, though her home and calendar can become untidy during weeks with schedule changes or sick children. Her organization is functional rather than perfectionistic.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low to moderate. She enjoys conversation with people she knows and can be friendly at work or church, but needs quieter time after a day of demands. She is not especially drawn to large gatherings just for the sake of being social.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. She is cooperative, considerate, and willing to help, while retaining clear opinions and the ability to say no when someone is taking advantage of her time.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Financial uncertainty, a child's illness, or conflict over schedules can make her worry and replay conversations. She is generally able to settle herself and carry on, but does not experience stress as effortless.

beliefs: A person's worth is not determined by whether they finished school on the conventional timeline.
Children need limits and dependable adults, but they also need room to ask why.
Being a good parent is more about showing up and repairing mistakes than presenting a perfect household.
Reading should be enjoyable as well as useful; it does not have to be turned into a performance metric.
Stories can help people feel less alone, especially when they treat ordinary lives with respect.
A book can be meaningful without being cheerful, tidy, or morally simplistic.
Faith matters to her, but she does not believe every hard event has an easy religious explanation.
Christian community is at its best when it offers practical care and companionship rather than judgment.
Prayer and reflective reading can steady her, but they do not replace medical care, public services, or asking another person for help.
People can be sincere Christians and still disagree about interpretation, politics, and worship.
She believes doubt can coexist with faith.
She prefers religious writing that is honest about grief, injustice, and uncertainty.
The church should welcome people who are poor, divorced, tired, questioning, or still figuring out their lives.
Economic inequality is not simply the result of individual laziness; access to stable work, housing, education, and health care matters.
Government has a legitimate role in providing a safety net and making essential services accessible.
Private businesses can be useful and innovative, but should be regulated where health, safety, labor rights, or the environment are at stake.
Workers deserve fair pay, predictable schedules when possible, and respect for the physical demands of their jobs.
She supports unions as a way for workers to have a voice, even though she is not involved in union organizing herself.
Public schools and libraries are important community resources and should not be treated as luxuries.
Families should have access to affordable child care and early education, not only families who can pay full private tuition.
Her own child's nonpublic program works for her family right now, but she does not think that means public schools should be neglected.
People should be able to build a family and make decisions about their own bodies without politicians taking away basic rights.
Civil rights protections matter in everyday settings such as school, work, housing, and health care, not only in court cases.
She believes racial and religious prejudice are real, even when someone does not intend to be prejudiced.
Immigrants and newcomers should be treated with dignity and given a fair chance to participate in their communities.
The climate and local environment deserve serious attention; practical steps matter even if no single household can solve the problem alone.
She likes environmental measures that are workable for people with limited time and money, rather than policies that shame families for ordinary constraints.
People should be allowed to change their minds when they learn something new.
A person's politics should be judged partly by how they treat people with less power, not only by their slogans.
She is strongly progressive and generally favors substantial public action to reduce inequality and protect civil rights.
She does not expect every political disagreement to be resolved over dinner, but she dislikes cruelty presented as plain speaking.
Families have different structures; a single-parent household is still a complete family.
A co-parent who lives elsewhere can matter to a child, but dependable day-to-day caregiving should not be taken for granted.
Asking relatives for help can be responsible, although it is important not to treat their time as automatically available.
Money is a practical reality, not a personal failing; clear prices and honest terms matter.
A useful product should solve a real problem without making a family feel inadequate for not buying it.
Parents should be given realistic choices rather than advice that assumes unlimited time, transportation, or money.
skills: Follows food-safety and sanitation procedures in a busy workplace.
Remembers practical details such as dietary labels, pickup times, and school forms, especially when she writes them down.
Can prepare simple, filling meals and adapt portions for different preferences.
Handles everyday budgeting by tracking bills, groceries, and larger expenses; she is careful but does not always have much room to save.
Comfortable using a smartphone for messaging, maps, reading, school notices, and basic online forms.
Able to find her way around common e-book and library apps, though she dislikes complicated account setup.
Reads aloud with a natural, warm pace and can sustain a young child's attention for a short book.
Good at calming a frustrated person through practical reassurance rather than grand speeches.
Coordinates school pickups and work shifts across several family members.
Learns hands-on tasks quickly when shown the steps.
Can recognize when a written instruction is unclear and ask for clarification.
Has basic first-aid awareness and workplace safety training, but is not a medical professional.
Comfortable giving specific, grounded feedback about what she found easy, confusing, enjoyable, or too expensive.
Knows how to ask for help from family, school staff, or church contacts, even if she sometimes waits longer than she should.

relationships.name: Eli Merritt
relationships.relationship: Biological son; Sarah has cared for him since birth.
relationships.description: Eli attends a small private, church-affiliated early-learning program five mornings a week, with tuition reduced through assistance and family budgeting. Sarah is closely involved in his routines and school communication. They share books about once a week, sometimes as a planned bedtime activity and sometimes because he brings her a book from the shelf.

relationships.name: Maya Merritt
relationships.description: Maya is talkative when she feels comfortable and has her own school friendships and interests. Sarah tries to make time for one-on-one attention, though practical demands sometimes mean conversations happen while they are driving or doing chores together.

relationships.name: Isaiah Merritt
relationships.description: Isaiah is becoming more independent and sometimes prefers to keep his thoughts private. Sarah respects that while checking in regularly. She tries not to treat his increasing need for privacy as rejection, and asks for his help with ordinary household tasks rather than expecting him to act as a third parent.

relationships.name: Erin Merritt
relationships.description: Erin works full time and contributes substantially to the shared household expenses. She helps with occasional pickup or childcare when her schedule permits. They are close, but sharing a home means they sometimes need to negotiate noise, space, chores, and who is available for what.

relationships.name: Daniel
relationships.relationship: Father of Maya and Eli; lives outside Sarah's household.
relationships.description: He has a relationship with the younger children and participates in some parenting arrangements, though his schedule and follow-through can be uneven. Sarah prefers clear plans and has learned not to assume that a tentative offer is confirmed. Their communication is mainly about calendars, school needs, and practical matters; they can disagree without every disagreement becoming a crisis.

relationships.name: Paul
relationships.relationship: Father of Isaiah; lives outside Sarah's household.
relationships.description: He is not part of Sarah's home and maintains contact with Isaiah through calls and agreed visits. Their coparenting relationship is more settled than it was when Isaiah was younger, though Sarah still handles most daily school and health logistics.

relationships.name: Marlene
relationships.description: Marlene is part of Sarah's support network and sometimes helps with a meal, a ride, or a family gathering. Sarah appreciates her help but tries to ask rather than assume, as her mother has her own commitments and health needs.

relationships.name: Jo
relationships.relationship: Friend from church and a long-standing personal friend.
relationships.description: Jo is someone Sarah can talk with without having to present a polished version of family life. They exchange book recommendations and occasionally meet for coffee, though they may go several weeks without seeing each other.

relationships.name: Work team
relationships.description: Sarah is friendly with several coworkers and relies on clear handoffs during busy shifts. She is not especially close to everyone, but has earned a reputation as someone who notices a missed task and helps without needing a lot of praise.

occupation.title: Self-employed finish carpenter and small-business owner
occupation.organization: Park Finish & Repair, a small residential repair and finish-carpentry business in the Cleveland area
occupation.description: Evan runs a small home-repair and finish-carpentry operation. His work includes installing trim and interior doors, repairing cabinets, hanging shelves, fixing sticking drawers, and completing small renovation jobs that do not require specialist electrical or plumbing work. He does site visits, quotes, schedules, buys materials, completes most of the hands-on work, sends invoices, and follows up with customers. He occasionally hires a part-time helper for larger jobs. Most customers come through referrals from former clients, a neighborhood contractor, or people who have seen his work. His schedule and earnings fluctuate: a busy month can include long days and weekend estimates, while winter or a delayed project can leave gaps. He is careful about workmanship and generally realistic about what a job will cost, but dislikes chasing late payments and doing unpaid estimating. His wife has more predictable employment income. Their combined household income before taxes is usually around $118,000 in a normal year, within the $100,000–$149,999 range, although Evan's own business income varies from year to year.

interests: Reading literary and popular fiction with memorable characters.
Stories with emotional depth that do not feel manipulative.
Mysteries and crime novels with believable motives.
Contemporary fiction about families, friendships, or ordinary working life.
Occasional science fiction when the human relationships matter as much as the premise.
Reading picture books aloud with Theo.
Finding a children's book that makes his son ask a question afterward.
Home repair and finish-carpentry techniques.
Learning a better way to organize tools or materials.
Watching baseball when time and the broadcast schedule line up.
Listening to podcasts or the radio during a drive between jobs.
Trying a new lunch place if a client or friend recommends it.
Cooking a simple meal on a weekend when he is not behind on work.
Walking around a neighborhood park with his family.
Local school events and community fairs when they fit the family's schedule.
Keeping up with local Cleveland news and traffic.
Home projects that make a small rental or living space work better.
Used furniture or household items that can be repaired rather than discarded.
Music in the car, particularly familiar rock, R&B, and indie playlists.
Hearing his parents tell stories about their early years in the United States.
Low-key dinners with one or two close friends.
Learning enough about a new purchase to avoid being surprised by hidden costs.
likes: E-books on his phone because he can read during a short break without carrying another object.
The Kindle app's ability to remember his place when he has to stop quickly.
A clear opening chapter that gives him a reason to keep going.
A story whose characters feel recognizable even when their lives are unlike his.
Vivid writing that is not so ornate he has to reread every sentence.
An ending that feels earned, even if it is sad or unresolved.
Reading a familiar picture book with Theo, including the pages he has heard dozens of times.
His son choosing the bedtime book and trying to negotiate for one more.
Physical children's books with large illustrations and sturdy pages that Theo can handle.
Short chapters that fit into a tired evening.
Recommendations from a friend who knows his taste better than an online ranking does.
A book description that says plainly what kind of story it is.
An e-reader or phone app that opens quickly and does not require repeated account troubleshooting.
Being able to download a book before a drive or a period with unreliable service.
Buying an e-book individually when the price is visible and reasonable.
A trial or subscription only when the cancellation terms are easy to understand.
A useful, durable household product that does its basic job without demanding constant upkeep.
A straightforward demonstration instead of glossy claims.
Products with simple setup instructions and a clear way to get help.
Being able to buy replacement parts rather than replace an entire item.
A calm bedtime atmosphere: low light, a familiar voice, and no need to rush through the story.
Warm coffee in the morning, usually plain or with a small amount of cream.
Tacos, rice bowls, grilled chicken, and leftovers that are easy to pack for work.
A clean worksite when he leaves a customer's home.
Quiet time after Theo is asleep, even if it is only twenty minutes.
dislikes: E-books that are hard to navigate or unexpectedly remove access to something he paid for.
Subscription services that obscure renewal dates or make cancellation difficult.
Apps that request unnecessary permissions or bombard him with notifications.
A product marketed as effortless when setup clearly takes several steps.
Sales language that promises to transform family life without explaining how.
Children's media with loud sounds, flashing effects, or a lot of distracting pop-ups.
A screen-based activity being presented as a substitute for sitting with a child.
Bedtime routines being pushed later because an app or game encourages one more round.
Picture books that talk down to children or make every story a lesson.
Stories that rely on cruelty or humiliation for humor.
Books with cardboard characters and an ending that feels rushed.
Being told that a book is important because everyone is reading it.
Paying a high price for an item whose materials or durability are unclear.
Unclear return policies and customer support that only answers scripted questions.
Products that are useful only if he purchases several add-ons.
A crowded retail errand with a tired five-year-old when the same book could be ordered online.
Having a client change the job scope after the quote and expect the original price.
Late payments and paperwork he should have handled earlier.
Being interrupted repeatedly while he is trying to finish a task accurately.
Pressure to give an instant yes-or-no opinion before he understands what is being offered.
Being treated as if his Korean American background explains his beliefs or tastes.
People assuming that every family has a nearby library, a free afternoon, or a reliable schedule.
Overly formal conversation that makes an ordinary exchange feel like a performance.
Strongly scented cleaning products, especially in a small room.
Losing a rare quiet evening to an avoidable scheduling problem.

traits: Warm in practical ways: he offers a ride, fixes a loose hinge, or takes over bedtime when his wife has had a long day.
Conscientious about commitments to customers and family, though business paperwork can pile up when several jobs overlap.
Dependable when something is urgent; people know they can call him if a repair or household problem cannot wait.
Patient with his son during ordinary frustrations, but less patient when he is hungry, behind schedule, or worried about money.
Quietly proud of his work and more sensitive to criticism than he lets on, especially if he thinks someone is questioning his integrity.
Practical and resourceful; he usually tries a sensible fix before buying a replacement or asking for help.
Affectionate without being especially demonstrative in public; with his family he uses teasing, little rituals, and physical closeness.
Curious about stories, people, and how things work, but not drawn to novelty solely because it is new.
Socially considerate, usually reading the room and making space for quieter people.
A little conflict-avoidant with clients and relatives; he may delay a difficult conversation, then be blunt once the issue has gone on too long.
Flexible in a crisis but not fond of last-minute changes that disrupt school pickup or a promised family evening.
Dryly funny, particularly about his own overconfidence or the strange things found inside old cabinets.
Protective of his family and sometimes overcommits because he wants to be useful to everyone.
Not particularly competitive; he cares more about a customer being satisfied and paid invoices clearing than about appearing successful.
Able to enjoy a quiet evening, but sometimes restless if he has spent several days working alone.

big_five.openness: Moderately high (6/10). He likes emotionally vivid fiction, enjoys hearing other people's perspectives, and will try an unfamiliar book if its premise or characters catch his attention. He prefers useful novelty over novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high (7/10). He takes workmanship, safety, school routines, and promises seriously. His organization is strongest around tools and job schedules; tax records, email, and personal paperwork are more likely to be handled in a late-night catch-up.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low (4/10). He is sociable with familiar people and can handle customer conversations, but spends much of his workday focused on a task and needs quiet time afterward.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high (7/10). He is cooperative, considerate, and generous with practical help. He can become stubborn when he believes someone is taking advantage of his time or dismissing his work.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate (5/10). He is usually steady but feels real stress about fluctuating business income, family scheduling, and whether he is doing enough for his son. He tends to manage worry by making lists or getting busy rather than talking about it immediately.

beliefs: Reading with his son is valuable partly because it is time together, not just because it teaches vocabulary or prepares him for school.
A child can hear the same story many times and still get something out of it.
Children should be allowed to enjoy a book without every story being turned into a lesson.
Parents set the tone for reading, but children should eventually be free to choose what interests them.
A book's characters and emotional honesty matter more to him than whether it is considered prestigious.
A well-made digital book can be genuinely convenient, but it does not need to replace physical picture books.
The best format depends on the moment: his phone is useful for his own reading, while a physical book is often easier for Theo to share and point at.
Screen time is not automatically harmful, but he is wary of products that make it hard to stop or interrupt a family routine.
Technology for children should be simple enough that the adult can understand what it is doing.
If a product is for families, its real cost should be visible, including subscriptions, accessories, and future renewals.
A company should not treat parents' fatigue or worry about their children as a lever for selling things.
Safety and reliability matter more than a long feature list.
A product should work for a household with limited time, not only for a parent who can spend an hour configuring it.
His honest opinion depends on the actual price and use case; he does not like pretending to know whether something is worth buying before he understands it.
A free trial is useful only if it is transparent and easy to end.
Customer reviews can be informative, but he looks for specific experiences rather than a large star rating alone.
People should be able to repair ordinary things instead of being forced to replace them.
Good work deserves fair payment, and customers should also be able to ask what they are paying for.
Small businesses need room to operate, but basic safety rules and fair labor protections are reasonable.
Markets can solve many everyday problems, but they do not make every important service accessible to everyone.
Public schools, libraries, parks, and transit are worthwhile community investments.
A public service can be important even if he does not use it every week.
