Comfortable using a basic handheld scanner and routine inventory screens after on-the-job training.
Knows how to keep a work area and aisle clear and follows basic lifting and safety practices.
Good at explaining where common store items are and asking a customer a few questions to understand what they need.
Can handle everyday household fixes such as tightening a loose handle, assembling simple furniture, and replacing basic hardware, while recognizing when a job needs a professional.
Able to plan family errands around school pickup, work shifts, and the household vehicle schedule.
Can keep a bedtime story engaging by varying his voice slightly, noticing Mateo's reactions, and pausing for questions.
Speaks conversational Spanish and can follow ordinary family conversation, though he is slower reading complex Spanish text.
Uses a smartphone for e-books, maps, messaging, school updates, and everyday purchases.
Good at following a story's clues and remembering a minor detail that later becomes important.
Can prepare several simple family meals and make practical use of leftovers.
Learns best through demonstrations, repetition, and direct feedback rather than dense manuals.

relationships.name: Luz Alvarez
relationships.description: Luz and Gabriel have been together for many years and share a home and two children. She works full time in billing and administration at a dental office. She is more consistent about calendars and paperwork; Gabriel tends to handle practical errands and hands-on tasks. They sometimes disagree about clutter, spending, or how much structure the children need, but usually settle the disagreement privately and divide the work.

relationships.name: Mateo Cohen
relationships.description: Gabriel cared for Mateo from birth and is involved in his daily routines. Mateo is curious, energetic, and fond of repeat books. Gabriel enjoys reading with him and tries not to make bedtime feel like a performance or lesson.

relationships.name: Elena Cohen
relationships.description: Elena is increasingly independent and has her own school, friends, and interests. Gabriel gives her room but checks in about transportation, school plans, and how things are going. He knows she sometimes finds his questions repetitive, but he sees them as a way of staying involved.

relationships.name: Irene Rivera
relationships.description: Puerto Rican, family-oriented, and a regular source of Spanish-language conversation and family history. Gabriel calls or visits when schedules permit. She passed along some children's books and family stories, although her own religious background is not the same as Gabriel's Jewish identity.

relationships.name: David Cohen
relationships.description: Jewish and part of the family background through which Gabriel learned about Jewish holidays and customs. Their relationship is affectionate but not always emotionally demonstrative. His father encouraged him to read mysteries when he was young.

relationships.name: Rosa
relationships.description: A cousin on his mother's side who shares family updates, recipes, and recommendations. She is one of the people Gabriel will ask if she knows about a local event or has a book the children might like.

relationships.name: Darnell
relationships.description: A more experienced stockroom coworker who showed Gabriel some of the store's inventory routines. They trade practical tips and jokes during quieter shifts but are not close outside work.

Omar Rafael Morales.nationality: American; U.S. citizen of Puerto Rican and broader Hispanic/Latino heritage

occupation.title: Part-time grocery stock and receiving associate
occupation.organization: A neighborhood grocery store in the West Haven area
occupation.schedule_and_income: Usually works about 20 to 24 hours a week, with shifts that vary depending on deliveries and staffing. His annual wages are modest, generally around $20,000 to $22,000 before taxes when hours are available. He is an employee rather than a contractor and does not have a college-based profession.
occupation.responsibilities: He helps unload smaller deliveries, checks that boxes and refrigerated goods are placed correctly, rotates stock so older items are used first, faces shelves, and helps customers find ordinary products. He may cover the register briefly when the store is short-staffed, but his main work is stocking and keeping the back room orderly.
occupation.skills_and_pressures: He knows how to notice damaged packaging, misplaced price labels, and food that is nearing its date. He is dependable about showing up when scheduled, but he has limited control over shift changes and does not always receive the hours he would prefer. The work involves standing and lifting, which can aggravate his knees and back. He appreciates a steady routine and familiar coworkers but would not describe the job as a calling.
occupation.workplace_manner: He is polite and helpful with customers, especially older people who need a shelf or item pointed out. He does not enjoy being hurried by a manager while also being expected to do a careful job, and he will quietly ask which task should take priority rather than guess.

interests: Practical nonfiction that explains how something works.
Books about history, especially social history and ordinary people's lives.
Personal finance advice that is realistic for a low-income household rather than aimed at investors.
Basic home and car repair information.
Health information that is clearly sourced and not alarmist.
Religious reading and discussions about faith in everyday life.
Memoirs by people whose lives differ from his own.
Local history and neighborhood stories.
Learning about other countries and migration histories.
Cooking inexpensive meals with familiar ingredients.
Watching baseball when a game is convenient.
Listening to call-in radio or practical interview programs during chores.
Taking Yusuf to the library and letting him choose books.
Talking with older relatives about family history.
Seeing Yusuf become more confident with words and stories.
Walking near the shoreline or through a park when the weather is mild.
Small repairs that make an item last longer.
Community events where children are welcome and there is no expensive admission.
Reading short articles about public services, schools, and local decisions.
Finding useful information without needing a paid subscription.
Comparing prices and checking whether a product can be repaired.
Quiet conversation after the household has settled for the night.
reading_preferences: He reads for learning and practical knowledge, not only to pass time.
He often chooses an informative book if he wants to understand a subject he has heard about but does not know well.
He reads several days a week, usually in short stretches of 10 to 25 minutes.
He prefers print, especially paperbacks and library hardcovers, because it is comfortable to pick up and put down.
He borrows a substantial share of his books from the public library.
He also uses mosque lending shelves, neighborhood exchanges, and used-book sales when available.
He likes a clear table of contents, a legible type size, and chapters that can be read independently.
He appreciates an author who explains unfamiliar terms without making the reader feel foolish.
He is more likely to finish a book that has useful examples than one that stays abstract for too long.
He reads English most easily, can follow some Spanish-language material, and is gradually building familiarity with Arabic reading.
He owns an English translation of the Qur'an and returns to passages or commentary rather than treating it like a book to race through.
He is interested in reflective Muslim writing about patience, family, generosity, and daily conduct.
He prefers religious books that explain context and invite thought over ones that rely on scolding.
He does not mind a book that challenges him, but he wants the writer to show how the argument was reached.
He checks books out in small batches because he has limited uninterrupted reading time.
He sometimes uses a library audiobook when his eyes are tired, but it is not his default format.
He does not pay for many digital reading services and dislikes an e-book that is difficult to navigate on a phone.
He likes books with a clear index or glossary if he expects to refer back to them.
He will reread a short passage he found useful and sometimes mentions it to Farah.
He enjoys picture books with Yusuf, especially ones with rhythm, repetition, or an engaging factual detail.
For Yusuf, he likes stories about animals, vehicles, families, everyday feelings, and children solving small problems.
He appreciates children's books that show Muslim, Latino, and multiracial families without making identity the only subject.
He likes having a few familiar bedtime books alongside new library choices.
He does not expect a children's book to teach a lesson on every page; a funny or comforting story is worthwhile too.
likes: A library that is welcoming to children and does not make borrowing feel like a luxury.
Books with sturdy pages and covers that survive repeated use.
Clear, plain explanations with enough detail to be useful.
A book or product that can be borrowed, shared, repaired, or passed along.
A good cup of tea after Yusuf is asleep.
Rice, beans, soups, and other meals that can stretch across more than one dinner.
Fresh bread from a nearby shop when the household budget permits.
A quiet morning before errands begin.
Neighborhood stores where staff recognize regular customers.
People who answer a question directly instead of giving a long sales pitch.
A printed receipt and a clear return policy.
Being able to compare a price with a less expensive alternative.
A modest family gathering with food and room for the child to play.
Visiting relatives without needing an elaborate itinerary.
Gentle humor that does not embarrass someone else.
Useful reminders from school that arrive with enough notice.
A well-organized shelf or pantry after a busy week.
Walking outdoors when it is not too hot or icy.
A book that gives him a new fact he can share with Yusuf.
Children's products that do not require a complicated setup.
Arabic words and phrases Yusuf picks up and uses proudly.
Having a plan for the week, even if the plan has to change.
dislikes: Subscription fees that are easy to start and hard to cancel.
A price shown without taxes, add-ons, or the cost of necessary supplies.
Products that are marketed as essential for good parenting.
Overly complicated instructions, especially when a simple diagram would help.
Books with tiny print or dense pages that make reading feel like work.
Religious writing that uses shame as its main form of persuasion.
Children's stories that are frightening without a clear reason.
Books that present one kind of family as the only normal one.
Digital products that need a fast internet connection to function.
Unnecessary screen time for a four-year-old.
Fragile toys or book accessories that break after a few weeks.
A sales representative who assumes he will buy something because he likes the idea.
Being rushed to answer a question he has not fully understood.
People treating library use as a sign that a family cannot value books.
Unexpected work-schedule changes that disrupt childcare.
Standing in a long line with a tired child and no place to sit.
Food waste, particularly when a household has worked hard to buy groceries.
Being told that careful budgeting alone can solve low wages or high rent.
Crowded, noisy places where Yusuf cannot stay focused.
Excessive packaging that adds cost but does not protect the item.
new_product_decision_preferences: He wants to know the full price before being asked whether he likes a concept.
He considers whether the product solves a real household problem or merely adds another task.
He is more persuaded by a clear demonstration than by broad claims about innovation.
He notices whether a product is safe and suitable for a four-year-old.
He wants to know whether an adult has to supervise it continuously.
He considers how durable it is and what happens if a part goes missing.
He values straightforward instructions and setup that can be done without special tools.
He is wary of recurring charges and accounts that require a credit card.
He wants a low-cost option or a way to try the product before making a commitment.
He appreciates a clear return, repair, or replacement policy.
He notices whether the product works offline or depends on a phone and internet access.
He cares whether it can be used by someone who is not comfortable with technology.
He would rather hear a modest, specific claim than an exaggerated promise.
He may ask how the product compares with something the library, school, or community already provides.
He considers storage space because the apartment is not large.
He responds positively to useful features that do not make the product harder to use.
He does not assume a premium appearance means better value.
He is interested in language access when it is relevant, particularly Arabic and English options.
He wants to know who the intended user is and whether the product is actually designed for a family like his.
He is willing to give candid feedback, including saying that a concept is appealing but too expensive.

traits: Practical: he naturally asks what a thing is for and whether it will solve an actual problem.
Cautious: he checks details and thinks through downside risks before committing household money.
Patient with children: he can repeat a story or answer the same question several times, though fatigue makes him less patient late at night.
Protective: he is attentive to Yusuf's safety and tends to plan around the child's needs.
Quietly curious: he enjoys learning about unfamiliar subjects when the information is understandable and connected to real life.
Modest: he does not like presenting himself as an authority and readily says when he does not know something.
Persistent: he will keep trying to resolve a form, repair, or practical problem even when the process is frustrating.
Warm but reserved: affection is more often shown through time, rides, food, and follow-through than grand declarations.
Fair-minded: he will listen to a different view, although he is less open to opinions that dismiss the struggles of people with little money.
A little stubborn: once he has decided a purchase is not worth its cost, a sales pitch rarely changes his mind without new evidence.
Self-conscious about age: he sometimes worries that he will have less energy than younger parents as Yusuf gets older, but he does not want to make the child responsible for reassuring him.
Dryly humorous: he uses understated jokes, often about his own forgetfulness or the number of library books that have accumulated by the bed.
Community-oriented: he feels responsibility toward relatives, neighbors, and people from the mosque, though he must balance that with his immediate household.
Sensitive to condescension: he reacts poorly when someone assumes that a low income means he is careless, uninformed, or uninterested in quality.
Emotionally steady in public: he tends to contain worry and handle the next task first, then talk about stress with Farah or a trusted friend.

big_five.openness: Medium to moderately high. He likes informative books and is willing to learn about unfamiliar topics, but favors ideas he can connect to lived experience over novelty for its own sake.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high. He is reliable about work, school routines, and bills he can pay, though limited resources and changing shifts make his plans less orderly than he would like.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He is not socially anxious, but he prefers small gatherings, familiar people, and conversations with a purpose over busy or performative social settings.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is considerate and cooperative, but not compliant; he will speak up when he thinks a proposal is unfair or impractical.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He has understandable financial and health worries, especially when a bill or shift is uncertain, but usually keeps functioning and tries to break problems into manageable steps.

beliefs: A parent should make a child feel safe and loved, even when the family cannot afford every opportunity it would like.
Being an older father has practical challenges, but it does not make him less committed to Yusuf.
Children benefit from a steady routine, while also needing room to be playful and unpredictable.
Reading aloud is worthwhile even before a child understands every word.
A child should see books as enjoyable and useful, not as a test of whether they are smart.
Public libraries are essential public institutions, not merely places to borrow books.
Families should not have to buy every educational resource their children need.
A good children's book can entertain first and still leave a child with something to think about.
Children should see different cultures, languages, and kinds of families represented in ordinary stories.
Language learning is a strength; a child who speaks more than one language should not be treated as confused or behind.
Arabic and English can both be part of Yusuf's sense of home, and Spanish remains part of Omar's family history.
Faith should help a person act with patience, honesty, generosity, and humility.
Muslim practice can be sincere even when work, health, and family responsibilities affect how regularly someone attends a mosque.
Religious questions deserve thoughtful answers rather than intimidation.
He does not believe one has to erase Puerto Rican or Latino identity to be a Muslim.
People from different religious backgrounds should be able to live together without being treated as suspicious.
A person's faith is personal, but it also carries responsibilities toward neighbors and people in need.
People should be able to disagree about politics without assuming the other person is evil or stupid.
Compromise is useful when it produces a workable result, but compromise should not mean ignoring people who are consistently left out.
He considers himself politically moderate or centrist, though his views do not fit neatly into one party's platform.
Government should substantially reduce economic inequality through progressive taxation, public services, and social protections.
People with much greater means can reasonably pay a higher share in taxes if the revenue supports services that benefit the public.
Public early-childhood programs help children and working families, and should be funded reliably.
Healthcare and basic medicines should not become inaccessible because a family has a low income.
Food assistance can help a family get through a difficult period and should not be treated as a moral failure.
A safety net should be available, but public programs should also be understandable and respectful to the people who use them.
Workers deserve predictable scheduling and fair pay, especially when employers depend on their reliability.
Hard work matters, but hard work alone cannot overcome every structural disadvantage.
Small businesses can be valuable parts of a neighborhood, while large employers still need to be accountable for how they treat workers.
Government spending should be scrutinized, but cutting every public service is not the same as responsible budgeting.
He values public safety, but believes fairness and accountability matter when authorities exercise power.
Immigration debates should recognize that families have complicated histories and should not be reduced to slogans.
A useful product should be priced for the people it claims to serve, not only for the most comfortable buyers.
A free or shared option can be valuable even when a paid product is better made; the comparison should be honest.
Parents should be given clear information about a product's cost, safety, and limitations rather than pressured through guilt.
A company should listen to criticism from ordinary customers, not only praise from people who can afford every new offering.
skills: Stock rotation, basic receiving procedures, and spotting damaged or expired goods.
Practical price comparison and household budgeting under tight constraints.
Finding useful books and community resources through a public library catalog or staff recommendation.
Reading aloud with expression and adjusting a story when Yusuf loses interest.
Keeping a simple household calendar for school dates, appointments, and shifts.
Basic food preparation, stretching ingredients, and using leftovers safely.
Minor household troubleshooting, such as tightening a loose handle or replacing a simple fixture when he has the right tool.
Speaking fluent English, conversational Spanish in familiar settings, and functional everyday Arabic.
Recognizing when he needs an expert rather than attempting a repair that could be unsafe.
Giving clear, grounded feedback about whether a product's instructions, price, or daily use seem realistic.
Staying calm with customers and coworkers when a small problem can be solved directly.
Using a smartphone for calls, text messages, school notices, maps, and basic online searches, though he dislikes doing lengthy forms on a small screen.

relationships.name: Farah Morales
relationships.description: Farah is 47 and grew up in a Palestinian-American family where Arabic was used at home. She is Yusuf's regular caregiver and currently has no steady paid job; most of her time goes to childcare, school routines, and household responsibilities. She and Omar share decisions, although they sometimes disagree about whether a small purchase is worth the cost. She is more fluent in Arabic, while Omar is more comfortable handling complicated paperwork in English. Their relationship has affectionate habits and ordinary strains, especially when money or sleep is short.

relationships.name: Yusuf Morales
relationships.description: Yusuf is Omar's only child and lives in the household. Omar was involved from birth and is an everyday caregiver, not a parent who is only present for occasional visits. Yusuf attends a public early-childhood program, enjoys picture books, and is beginning to recognize familiar words. He understands and uses both English and Arabic in age-appropriate ways; Omar speaks English with him and uses Arabic phrases and routines learned through the family.

relationships.name: Omar's mother and extended Puerto Rican family
relationships.relationship: Close relatives, most living in New York
relationships.description: Omar stays in contact by phone and occasional visits. Some relatives are Catholic or not especially religious, and the family does not all share his beliefs, but he remains attached to their food, humor, stories, and family history. Spanish is more present in this part of the family than in his household.

relationships.name: Farah's parents and siblings
relationships.relationship: In-laws and part of Yusuf's Arabic-speaking family network
relationships.description: They are an important source of language, family connection, and occasional practical help. Omar respects their role while sometimes feeling self-conscious about his imperfect Arabic or about not being able to contribute financially as much as he would like.

relationships.name: Hassan
relationships.relationship: Friend from the local Muslim community
relationships.description: Hassan is a longtime acquaintance who sometimes recommends short books or talks through a religious question with Omar. Their conversations are personal rather than formal instruction, and they do not agree about every social or political issue.

relationships.name: Tanya
relationships.description: Tanya has worked at the store longer and knows how to navigate its changing shifts. They exchange practical favors, such as telling one another about schedule changes, but are not close friends outside work.

relationships.name: Yusuf's early-childhood teacher
relationships.description: Omar appreciates teachers who give specific information about what Yusuf is learning and what the family can do at home without buying extra materials. He is polite at school events but can be quiet when many parents are talking at once.

relationships.name: Neighbors in the apartment building
relationships.description: Omar has friendly, limited relationships with several neighbors. They may watch for a delivery or pass along a community notice, but the family does not rely on neighbors for regular childcare.
